title: Reset Sleep Cycle
content: The Sleep Cycle Loop

These days, many people feel like they simply do not have enough time in their day. The day seems to pass faster and faster, while the workload keeps increasing. There is less time for yourself, less time for family, and sometimes even less time to properly enjoy life. But what if the problem is not always the amount of time we have? What if, at least in some cases, the way we shape our day is the real problem?

There can be many reasons behind an unorganized or unproductive day, but one of the most important ones I wanted to explore was the **sleep cycle**. We often underestimate how much our sleeping and waking times influence the rest of our day. A common pattern looks very simple: **you sleep late, so you wake up late; because you wake up late, your day feels shorter; because your day feels shorter, you stay awake longer to finish things or enjoy your free time; and because you stay awake longer, you sleep late again.** Then the same thing happens the next day.

This creates a loop that can become surprisingly difficult to escape. Modern life also sometimes glorifies staying awake late at night—going out at 2 or 3 AM, working late, scrolling endlessly, or simply treating late nights as a normal part of life. There is nothing inherently wrong with being awake at night, especially for people whose schedules genuinely require it. But when a late-night schedule consistently pushes your waking time later and leaves you with less usable daytime, it can start affecting how the entire day feels.

I experienced this myself during my experiment. Normally, I would sleep around midnight or, at the latest, somewhat later. But for the first part of the experiment, I deliberately pushed my sleep time much further—to around **3–4 AM**. As a result, I was waking somewhere around **8–11 AM**. I noticed that I felt less focused, and more importantly, it felt like my day was becoming smaller and smaller. I was technically still getting a substantial amount of time awake, but the way those hours were distributed made the day feel different.
That was the point where I wanted to test something: **What happens if you don't try to completely rebuild your life overnight, but instead break the loop at one point?**
Breaking the Loop

Breaking a sleep pattern is not necessarily easy. If your body has become accustomed to sleeping at 3 or 4 AM, suddenly deciding that you will sleep at 10 PM does not automatically make you sleepy at 10 PM. The challenge is not just choosing a new bedtime; it is creating conditions that make an earlier sleep time feel natural.

For my experiment, I wanted to see whether one strong change could help me move away from the late-night pattern. Instead of trying to force myself to sleep, I focused on changing what happened during the day—particularly my exposure to the outdoors, physical activity, and the transition from an active day into a calmer evening.
The basic idea was simple: **break the loop once, then make the new pattern easier to continue.**
My Experiment

I divided the experiment into two parts. In the first part, I intentionally shifted my sleep schedule much later than usual. For about a week, I allowed myself to sleep around **3–4 AM**, sometimes even later, and wake up around **8–11 AM**. This was not my normal routine; I was doing it specifically to observe what the experience felt like.

The result was not what I wanted. I felt less focused, and I had the strong impression that my usable day was shrinking. Even though I was awake for many hours, a large portion of the daytime had already passed by the time I started my day properly. As a student preparing for JEE, I spend a significant amount of time at my desk, so losing those morning hours made the day feel even more compressed.
Then came the second part.

One evening, I went outside for a cycling session. I spent roughly half an hour away from my usual environment, surrounded by nature and away from the constant presence of screens, desks, walls, and people. You could also do something similar through walking, jogging, or another form of outdoor activity—the cycling itself was not the only important part for me.
That half hour gave me something I had been missing: a deliberate break from my usual environment.
I wasn't going outside because I had somewhere to go. I wasn't going outside to complete a task. I was simply moving, experiencing the environment, and giving my mind some space.

When I returned home after cycling, I was naturally sweaty, so I took a shower. That created another interesting transition. The time outdoors had left me feeling mentally refreshed, while the shower made my body feel refreshed. Together, it felt like I had reset both sides of myself before returning to my work.

After that, I studied for JEE from around **8 PM to 10 PM**. Later, around **10:30 PM**, something happened that I wasn't trying to force: I started feeling sleepy naturally. After having been sleeping around 3–5 AM during the previous period, I eventually went to bed at around **11 PM**.
And the difference was noticeable.
I slept well and woke up around **5 AM** the next morning. More importantly, I didn't wake up feeling like I had dragged myself out of bed. I felt surprisingly fresh.
Why the Morning Matters

After that first successful break in the cycle, I started doing the outdoor activity in the **morning**, usually around 6–7 AM. This became much easier to continue because I was no longer trying to force my sleep schedule entirely through willpower.

One of the most interesting things I noticed was that I could start waking up around **4–6 AM without relying on an alarm**. This was something I had rarely experienced before. Even though I was waking significantly earlier than during my late-night experiment, I didn't feel as though I had lost energy. Instead, I often felt refreshed when I woke up.

There is also a practical reason why I found the morning approach useful. As a JEE aspirant, a large part of my day can easily become sitting at a desk, studying, solving problems, or staying indoors. If I spend almost the entire day inside the same environment, it is easy to lose the feeling of a natural day-night rhythm.

Going outside gives me a deliberate connection with daylight, movement, fresh air, and the changing environment around me. Our biological clock is influenced by environmental cues, especially the light-dark cycle, so regular exposure to daylight—particularly earlier in the day—can support a more consistent sleep-wake rhythm. My personal experiment was not a controlled scientific study, but it made this connection much more noticeable to me.
And this is where the idea of spending time in nature became important.

Think about people who live in environments where being outdoors is simply part of everyday life. They may wake up with the morning, experience daylight, move around during the day, and naturally become less active as the evening progresses. Modern indoor life can separate us from many of these environmental cues.

I'm not saying that everyone needs to move to a village or completely change their lifestyle. The idea is much simpler: **if you cannot bring your entire life closer to nature, you can at least give yourself a small amount of time to reconnect with it.**
For me, that was around half an hour.
Half an Hour to Reset

The biggest takeaway from this experiment wasn't that cycling magically fixes a sleep schedule. It was the combination of several small things happening at the right time: getting outside, moving my body, experiencing daylight and nature, taking a shower afterward, returning to focused work, and eventually allowing myself to become naturally tired at night.
That half hour became a kind of reset point in my day.
And that's the idea I want to take forward: **you don't always have to fix everything at once. Sometimes you just need to break the loop at one point.**
If your current pattern is:
**Sleep late → Wake late → Shorter-feeling day → Stay awake late → Sleep late**

then trying to change every part simultaneously can feel overwhelming. Instead, start by creating one strong interruption. Go outside. Walk. Cycle. Jog. Get some daylight. Give your mind a break from the desk. Let your body move. Then return and see how the rest of the day changes.

For me, that simple change helped me move from sleeping around 3–5 AM toward sleeping around 11 PM and waking much earlier. The experiment also reminded me that productivity is not simply about squeezing more hours into a day. Sometimes it is about **shaping those hours better**.
You may think you need more time.
But sometimes, you don't need more hours.
**You just need to reset the way your day begins.**
